Issued at 259 AM CDT Mon Jul 27 2026

     TODAY THROUGH LATE TUE NIGHT/EARLY WED AM...

Much like the previous few days, water vapor satellite imagery 
and upper air analysis shows a strong and large mid/upper ridge
across a large portion of the southern and central CONUS early
this morning. As a result, another day of very hot conditions 
will dominate much of the central plains today. Temperatures 
this morning have only dropped into the low to mid 80s (as of 
3AM) thanks to a persist southerly breeze keeping the boundary 
layer decently mixed overnight. Additionally, highs on Sunday 
outperformed the forecast once again, especially along and west 
of the I-135 corridor due to a deep and well-mixed boundary
layer eroding low-level moisture across these areas. With the 
day starting out as warm as it is along with expectation of 
similar conditions today compared to yesterday, afternoon highs 
for today were nudged up a bit from the NBM, especially across 
central Kansas where highs at or above 110 are not out of the 
realm of possibility. This could be further supported by modest 
compressional warming ahead of a weak cold front forecast to sag
into northern Kansas by this afternoon.

Heading into the evening and nighttime hours, this frontal boundary 
will become the focus for potential storm chances overnight into 
Tuesday morning. The aforementioned mid/upper ridge that has been 
the primary driver for this ongoing heatwave across the central
plains will begin to shift ever so slightly southwest during 
the day today. Meanwhile, a subtle shortwave trough embedded in 
weak northwest flow aloft will provide a source of modest 
synoptic ascent over the northern High Plains this evening into 
tonight. This along with upslope flow at the surface along the 
the slow-moving frontal boundary should trigger numerous storms
across northeast Colorado, northwest Kansas, and western 
Nebraska this evening into tonight. Short term guidance points
to this convection moving eastward along an axis of instability
generally located along and north of the frontal boundary 
(which should be in the vicinity of I-70 by late tonight). 
Pretty much all of the CAM guidance suggests that convection 
will manage to make its way into portions of central Kansas 
either very late tonight or into Tuesday morning. However, given
persistent very warm mid-level temperatures, any activity will 
likely struggle, and the intensity of this activity is not 
anticipated to be severe as a result. However, gusty winds 
cannot be ruled out, especially if convection begins to 
dissipate across northern and central Kansas.

With the mid/upper ridge continuing to shift southwest on Tuesday, a 
mid-level baroclinic zone is forecast to reside over the area with 
weak, but somewhat persistent, WAA expected along this feature.
As a result, isolated convection may fester across central and 
eastern Kansas for much of the day on Tuesday. Meanwhile, the 
previously mentioned weak frontal boundary will remain draped 
across the forecast area with temperatures along and south of 
this boundary expected to soar into the 100s once again Tuesday 
afternoon. With just a touch more moisture in the atmosphere, it 
appears likely heat indices will be between 105 to 110 along and
south of US-54 during the afternoon and early evening hours. By
Tuesday night, eyes will turn out west again as another loosely
organized complex of showers and storms appears likely to 
develop across the High Plains and march eastward overnight. 
However, similar to Tuesday morning, mid-level temperatures will
still be quite warm late Tuesday night/early Wednesday morning.
Thus, any convection coming off the High Plains will struggle 
as it moves eastward.

     WEDNESDAY THROUGH SUNDAY...

Assuming convection pans out as currently forecast Wednesday 
morning, much of the region will continue to feel the influence of 
the mid/upper ridge, which will be centered over the Four Corners 
Region by mid week. Thus, afternoon temperatures will still rise 
into the mid to upper 90s. Fortunately, dewpoints should only be in 
the upper 60s to low 70s, so Wednesday afternoon heat indices will 
be generally between 100 and 105, mainly across southern Kansas. 
With the mid/upper ridge located over the southwestern CONUS
weak northwest flow aloft will generally reside over the 
central plains for the second half of the week. Mid range 
guidance remains consistent with showing a parade of subtle 
shortwave troughs embedded within this flow progressing across 
the central plains Wednesday through Saturday. As a result, a 
few rounds of showers and storms are possible, mainly during the
overnight hours Wednesday through Saturday. Currently chances 
remain somewhat low given some uncertainty in the forecast, and 
at this time, severe weather appears unlikely. However, stay 
tuned for updates to the forecast over the coming days as 
details are subject to change. Regardless of storm chances at
